title: Partnership with the School

segments.spoken_text:
Now we turn to partnership with school. Keep that home observation in mind. Your child, your family and the school may each hold different parts of the picture. Bringing those together can help shape useful support.

People arrive with very different school experiences. Some relationships feel helpful, and others have been difficult. You can take part without sharing a personal account. Please keep staff, schools and children unidentifiable in group discussion.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 1; matching slide PDF page 1; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 85; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Look at the overlapping partnerships: family, school staff and support staff, with your child at the centre. Each person brings different knowledge and a different relationship. Who else belongs in that picture for your family: perhaps a grandparent, therapist or out-of-school-hours carer?

What is the shared purpose of these partnerships? How can your child's own communication help shape it? Take a moment to reflect or discuss, and pause if you'd like more time.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 2; matching slide PDF page 2; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 86; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: Keep your child at the centre as you consider the answer. No single person holds the whole picture. A useful partnership helps people understand each other's knowledge and agree on support that makes a difference to the child.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 2; matching slide PDF page 2; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 86; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
The Family-School Partnerships Framework recognises parents and families as children's first and continuing educators. Learning happens across settings, and a family's diversity and strengths matter to that learning.

The other principles include community involvement, mutual trust and shared responsibility, supported by committed and collaborative leadership. In an everyday conversation, look for respectful listening, clear information, your child's views and agreed next steps. Family knowledge and school knowledge are both needed from the beginning. Respectful listening is possible even when people see a situation differently.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 3; matching slide PDF page 3; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 87; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: What makes collaboration work? Think of a situation where people have worked well together, inside or outside school. What helped them listen and make a decision? Share a brief idea or reflect privately. Pause here if you would like time.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 4; matching slide PDF page 4; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 88; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: The slide brings together shared goals and values, mutual trust, consultation, curiosity and attention to different perspectives. Your child's voice belongs throughout. The phrase assume good intent may feel difficult if trust has been damaged. Trust needs action from both sides, and it can take time to rebuild. A possible opening is: how could we work together so school goes well for my child? That gives the conversation a purpose while leaving room to discuss what needs to change.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 4; matching slide PDF page 4; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 88; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
There are also responsibilities that sit behind these conversations. The Disability Discrimination Act protects people from discrimination because of disability, including in education. The Disability Standards for Education explain obligations to support access and participation on the same basis as students without disability.

Schools must consult the student, or an associate such as a parent or carer, when considering reasonable adjustments. Useful questions are: how will we be consulted? What adjustments are in place? How and when will they be reviewed?

This is general information, rather than advice about an individual legal situation. The Department of Education's plain-language resources explain these rights and responsibilities for families. They are a useful place to return to after the workshop.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 5; matching slide PDF page 5; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 89; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Power can sit in the way a meeting is arranged, the language used and who can make decisions. Familiarity with school systems, cultural and historical experiences of education, language and financial circumstances can also shape how a conversation feels.

Who sets the agenda? Whose knowledge gets heard? Is your child included in a way that works for them? What might need to change about the process? Naming these features can help us plan a more balanced conversation. We can examine the meeting itself without turning the discussion into a judgement about an identifiable person.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 6; matching slide PDF page 6; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 90; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Use the Power dynamics activity on page fifteen, or three sticky notes. First, describe an imbalance from a home perspective. On the second, consider one from a school perspective. On the third, suggest how the imbalance could be addressed.

Thinking about another perspective doesn't mean excusing poor practice. It helps us identify what could change in a conversation. You can share at your table, add anonymous notes under Home, School and Solutions, or keep your notes private. Pause now for the activity.

segments.spoken_text: Look again at the solutions. Could the agenda be shared earlier? Could language be clearer, a support person be included, or another way of contributing be available? Choose one idea that would make participation more workable. Keep it for the conversation plan later in this session.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 7; matching slide PDF page 7; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 91; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 15. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text: We're going to hear from Adon. As you watch, pay attention to what decisions were made and who made them. Notice the effect of being included, or not included, in decisions about your own experience.

segments.spoken_text: What impact did those decisions have on Adon? Make a note on page fifteen, or discuss the question briefly. Then consider how your child's preferences are asked for and heard. Pause here if you'd like more time.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.

segments.spoken_text: Children can have a say through the ways they communicate: words, drawings, typing, visual choices, gesture or other responses. We can ask what helps, what is hard and what they want a teacher to know. Their own perspective belongs in the conversation, including when it differs from what adults expected.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 8; matching slide PDF page 8; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 92; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 15. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Turn to What works on page sixteen. Think of a time you worked well with someone at school. What made it work? What did they do, and what did you do? If a school example is difficult to find, choose another helpful relationship or listen to ideas from others.

Talk at your table without naming staff or schools, and note anything worth carrying forward. Pause for that reflection.
segments.screen_cue: Pause the video for the activity. Resume for the debrief.

segments.spoken_text: The practical moves on the slide are useful starting points: prepare, share information, ask questions and seek clarification. You can ask for an agenda beforehand, arrange to bring a support person and bring your own notes. Ask for a record of agreed actions, then follow up in writing so everyone can check what was understood. If trust is strained, a clear purpose and a small agreed step may be a beginning.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 9; matching slide PDF page 9; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 93; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 16. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Consultation is more useful when there is a clear shared purpose, open questions and more than one way to contribute. Your knowledge and your child's knowledge deserve attention. What was heard needs to be recorded accurately, followed by an agreed action, responsibility and follow-up.

The checklist on page sixteen can help before and after a meeting. Ask, listen and follow up. Before leaving, check who will do what and when you will hear how it is going. A conversation becomes more useful when everyone understands the next step.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 10; matching slide PDF page 10; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 94; full speaker notes. PC Primary - Workbook PDF page 16. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
The Working Together Communication Tool, on the left, helps you agree how home and school will communicate. You can choose a method, such as email, phone or a communication book, then record how often, what you'll communicate about, and the next dates or steps.

The Partnership Planning Template, on the right, asks what has worked, what has been challenging and what could help. You can use those prompts before a meeting or complete them together. A tool gives the conversation a place to start. Keep listening and your child's own communication alongside it.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 11; matching slide PDF page 11; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 95; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
The N C C D Meetings Tool Kit is a free resource for families and schools preparing for meetings about adjustments. It covers before, during and after a meeting.

The link is in the resources at the back of your workbook. You can use it to think about what information to bring and what to clarify. Your school may have its own process, so ask how consultation and follow-up will work in your setting.
segments.source_note: Parents and Carers - Primary, Session 5, slide 12; matching slide PDF page 12; PC Primary - Facilitator Guide PDF page 96; full speaker notes. Authored audience-facing delivery, with optional participation and no invented participant responses.

segments.spoken_text:
Help is available beyond this workshop. Autism Connect offers autism information and support. Disability Gateway helps people find disability information and services. Carer Gateway provides support for carers. Their contact details are at the back of your workbook.

Lifeline's crisis support number is thirteen, eleven, fourteen. Kids Helpline provides counselling for children and young people aged five to twenty-five on eighteen hundred, fifty-five, eighteen hundred. Its website also has information for parents and carers, and points parents towards Parentline for parenting counselling.

Take a moment to note the support that is relevant to you. You don't have to work everything out by yourself.

segments.spoken_text:
Turn to page seventeen and choose one purposeful conversation with school. What needs to be understood? What question could open the conversation? How will your child's views be included? What could be decided together, and how will you follow up?

Use short notes. Bring in one idea from the power activity that could make the conversation more balanced. There is no need to share a sensitive situation. Pause here and give yourself time to prepare.

segments.spoken_text: Circle the question you want to open with. Keep these notes for Session Six. A small, specific next step is enough: one thing that needs to be understood, and a way to hear from your child as part of it.
